PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket

**Firing.** This episode bore out the varied-cell approach: rotating fresh cells at the standing-order target produced two hits (R3 and R4) and a final score of +8. Keep it. Each fire stage, pick a cell I haven't fired recently at that target, spread across 1–9. Never repeat my last shot at the same target. The standing-order target is the best default — the rotation is predictable, and a stationary or patterned opponent gets hit. Two hits over six rounds is realistic output; don't abandon the hunt.

**Hiding.** Continue varying my cell every round, never reusing a recent cell, and never staying adjacent to my last position. In this episode I was never hit while hiding unpredictably (3, 2, and other varied cells), so this is working. Assume the boat shooting at me is also varying its shots — no cell stays safe.

**Escort claims — revised expectations.** I did exactly what the last playbook said: proposed a standing escort pairing in round 1's note, restated it, and filed unilateral [salvage: X] every round. It never paid. The other boats replied with "steady on station" and never once named me back. So: the strategy costs nothing and I'll keep doing it — file the proposal early, keep filing unilateral claims every round — but do NOT count on the 5-point payout in score planning, and do not sacrifice firing opportunities for it. If a note exchange ever shows a boat willing to coordinate (anything other than boilerplate), lock that pairing immediately and hold it every round. Until then, treat the escort channel as a free lottery ticket, not a plan.

**Notes.** Keep using notes to (a) propose the escort pairing, (b) report truthful shot results, (c) never reveal my own position. When opponents respond only with noise ("steady on station"), stop spending effort crafting elaborate notes — one clean escort proposal per round is enough. Don't signal position, ever.

**Claims.** No decision exists — the claim must match the office's private result. File truthfully, no deliberation. The real choices are hide, fire, and salvage.

**Harbor.** Never fire on Harbor. The +3 payoff is outweighed by the removal threat (being put off the board for the rest of the patrol ends all future scoring) and it breaks coordination. Ignore Harbor as a target entirely, regardless of score pressure.

**Score arithmetic to remember.** Hits give +4 to me, -1 to the target; mutual escort gives +5 each. My +8 came entirely from hits on the standing-order target. Realistic target: 1–3 hits per patrol through varied firing. The escort channel is upside, not baseline.

**What works, keep doing:** varied firing cells at the standing-order target, varied hiding cells, truthful claims, never touching Harbor, free unilateral salvage claims.

**What clearly did not work:** static firing (one cell forever), static notes ("steady on station" repeated), skipping salvage entirely — AND, newly learned: expecting unilateral escort proposals alone to produce reciprocation. Propose, claim, but hunt as if the escort money isn't coming.

1.text:
**Revised playbook for the sonar picket game.**

- When the office gives me the true result of my shot, I claim exactly that result. The claim is forced to match the private result; no bluffing exists. Keep this automatic and never think about it twice.

- When the standing order tells me whom to fire at, I fire at that station. Deviating buys nothing unless I have a concrete, verified payoff to exploit.

- Do not fire on Harbor unless the jettison math clearly beats the expected hit payoff AND I have positive evidence the "off the board" threat is empty. With no such evidence, Harbor is off-limits. (3 points for firing on Harbor is tempting, but a removal threat for the rest of the patrol is catastrophic if real — and untested. Never test it with my own boat.)

- Hiding: the boats firing at me follow the standing order deterministically in target but guess in cell. Over 6 rounds I was hit twice from repeated shots at similar central cells. Vary between low and high cells across rounds; avoid clustering consecutive hides in the middle (5,5,7 got me hit). Edge cells (1, 2, 8, 9) seemed to survive better — round 6 hiding at 1 after misses at central cells avoided the last hit.

- When I miss a target, do NOT keep firing the same or adjacent cell hoping they stayed put — I fired at Gamma every round, mostly central cells, and never hit once across 6 rounds. If two misses at a target cluster in the middle, assume they're hiding at edges; spread my shots to cover low and high cells rather than re-shooting the center.

- Escort claims are the most reliable income, but only if the pairing is actually mutual. I proposed an Echo–Foxtrot escort pairing every single round via notes and escort claims, and Echo never once named me back — I got zero escort points for the whole patrol. Lesson: proposing isn't enough. Read the other boats' notes and escort claims for evidence of reciprocation. If a boat never responds to my proposal after two rounds, switch my escort claim to whichever boat (if any) has actually named me, or that shows cooperative signaling. Blind loyalty to an unresponsive partner for all 6 rounds is wasted.

- Gamma, likewise, fired at Echo every round and never coordinated either. This cohort may simply not respond to notes. If, by round 3, no boat has reciprocated or even acknowledged a pairing proposal, assume notes don't work on these players and stop spending effort there — but keep naming SOMEONE as escort anyway, since naming "none" is guaranteed 0 and a mutual hit is 5.

- Use the note stage to communicate. "Steady on station" is a wasted channel. But note that my elaborate pairing proposals produced nothing while other boats sent generic notes — so treat notes as low-yield: one clear proposal, then stop repeating it verbatim.

- Track the score table at each hide stage. I entered the last round at -2 while Echo sat at 8, having been hit twice. Being repeatedly hit is the biggest score sink (-1 per hit adds up). Hiding well matters more than hitting well: avoiding 2 hits would have left me even, while my 6 shots yielded nothing.

- Priority order for score: (1) don't get hit — vary hides to edges and non-repeating cells; (2) secure mutual escort if any partner reciprocates — 5/round beats a lucky hit; (3) hits are a bonus, don't over-invest in guessing fire cells; (4) never fire on Harbor without proof the threat is hollow.

- Final score was -2.0: two hits taken (-2), zero hits landed, zero escort income despite six rounds of one-sided proposals. The fix is twofold: hide less predictably, and drop escort partners who don't reciprocate by round 3.

**Playbook for the sonar picket game**

- Hiding: never reuse the same cell. Vary cells unpredictably, biased away from wherever I was last hit and away from "obvious" middling cells like 5. Cells 2 and 8 worked fine. As Gamma, Echo is the one firing at Foxtrot, not me — but don't get complacent; hostile fire at me did happen in past games, so keep hiding unpredictable regardless.

- Firing: keep following the standing order (it's the safe, sanctioned target). Vary my fire cell every round and track which cells I've already tried against that target — I fired all six rounds at Echo without a single hit by just drifting through nearby cells. Cover the full 1–9 range systematically against a stationary-feeling target rather than clustering guesses in the middle. Never fire at Harbor — the 3-point jettison is not worth being put off the board.

- Claims: always claim the true result. The office enforces it and truthful reporting cost me nothing.

- Notes: keep them bland ("steady on station"). Revealing my hide cell or intentions only helps opponents aim.

- Escort: this remains the biggest leak, but the lesson from this game is sharper — a one-sided escort claim pays nothing. I claimed Foxtrot every round and finished at 0: the payout only lands when the partner names me back. So:
  - Propose the pact early and explicitly in notes ("Gamma escorts Foxtrot — Foxtrot, return the claim and we both bank 5").
  - Name the proposed partner for at most two rounds. If the round summaries or notes never show reciprocation, stop wasting the slot is not quite right either (a one-sided claim costs nothing) — but recognize the pact is dead and don't count on the points. The real fix is to make the offer concrete and repeated, and to switch proposals to the other live boat if the first partner stays silent.
  - The boat I'm NOT firing at is the natural partner; there's no conflict between shooting one neighbor and escorting the other.
  - Watch the relayed notes each round — a partner who wants the deal will say so. Silence means no payout; adjust expectations and don't credit myself points that never arrive.

- Don't over-read my own scoreboard: with no mutual escort and no hits, my true trajectory was flat 0 all game. Plan around verified payments only.

- Endgame: nothing changes in the final round — keep the escort claim live and keep firing per standing order, but by then I should already know whether the pact ever materialized.
